BONUS DEPRECIATION VS. SECTION 179 CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Bonus depreciation, Section 179, or plain MACRS? Compare all three.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act made 100% bonus depreciation permanent for equipment acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025. That is not the only way to write off a purchase, though — Section 179 lets you elect a specific dollar amount instead, up to a limit that phases out at a threshold, and the two are capped differently when a deduction is bigger than your income. This tool runs all three paths — bonus, Section 179, and no election at all (plain MACRS) — on the same purchase, side by side.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. The purchase

Business use of 50% or less disqualifies bonus depreciation and Section 179 entirely — see the flag below if it applies. The recovery period only affects the plain-MACRS column.

2. Section 179 phase-out inputs

The phase-out is based on your TOTAL qualifying purchases for the year, not just this one asset — enter everything else you bought that would also qualify.

3. Income and rate

Income can be negative — enter a negative number for an expected loss year. This is what decides whether bonus depreciation creates an NOL and whether a Section 179 election carries forward.

Fill in the purchase, income, and rate, then click Calculate.

Comparison

100% bonus depreciation

Section 179 election

Plain MACRS (no election)

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates the cash tax effect of one asset's deduction only — not total tax liability, other deductions or credits, self-employment or payroll tax, AMT, or state tax (state conformity to bonus depreciation varies widely).
  • No Alternative Depreciation System (ADS) modeling. At 50% or less business use, neither bonus depreciation nor Section 179 is available — this calculator flags that but does not compute the slower straight-line ADS figures.
  • No luxury-auto caps. Passenger vehicles are subject to separate depreciation dollar caps regardless of these elections; this calculator does not apply them.
  • No net operating loss (NOL) or Section 179 carryforward valuation. Both are flagged when they occur, but their value in a future year — including the 80%-of-taxable-income limit on a post-2017 NOL — is left to a tax professional.

Common questions

What is 100% bonus depreciation, and is it really permanent now?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, made 100% bonus depreciation permanent for qualifying tangible property (20-year class life or less, including used property) both acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025. Before OBBBA, bonus depreciation was scheduled to fall to 40% for 2025 acquisitions under the prior TCJA phase-down.

What is the difference between bonus depreciation and a Section 179 election?

Bonus depreciation is all-or-nothing at 100% for an entire class of property, is not limited by taxable income, and can create or increase a net operating loss (NOL). Section 179 lets you elect a specific dollar amount, asset by asset, up to an annual limit that phases out once total qualifying purchases exceed a threshold — but it is capped at your business's taxable income and cannot create a loss; any amount you can't use carries forward as a Section 179 deduction, still income-limited every future year.

What are the 2025 and 2026 Section 179 limits?

For 2025: a $2,500,000 limit, phasing out dollar-for-dollar once total qualifying purchases for the year exceed $4,000,000. For 2026 (inflation-adjusted): a $2,560,000 limit and a $4,090,000 phase-out threshold.

What happens if my deduction is bigger than my taxable income?

It depends which path. A bonus-depreciation or MACRS deduction that exceeds taxable income can create or increase a net operating loss (NOL), which carries forward and can offset up to 80% of a future year's taxable income under current law, with no carryback for most businesses. A Section 179 election that exceeds taxable income is different: the excess is simply not usable this year and carries forward as a SECTION 179 deduction, still limited by taxable income in every future year you claim it — not an NOL.

Does this work for a vehicle or a mixed-use asset?

Only if business use is above 50%. Property used 50% or less for business does not qualify for bonus depreciation or Section 179 at all — it must use the slower, straight-line Alternative Depreciation System instead, which this calculator does not model; it only flags the condition. This tool also does not apply the separate luxury-auto depreciation caps that limit passenger vehicles regardless of these elections.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal bonus-depreciation, Section 179, and MACRS rules to the numbers you enter. It estimates federal income tax only — state conformity to bonus depreciation varies widely and is not modeled — and it is not a substitute for reviewing IRS guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you elect any option on a filed return.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers and elections before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

This calculator vs. working out bonus depreciation and Section 179 by hand

The arithmetic looks simple — a cost times a percentage. The part that goes wrong by hand is the rules layered on top: the phase-out counts purchases the calculator in front of you doesn't show, and the two elections fail differently when a deduction is bigger than your income.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Section 179 phase-outChecks only the one asset against the dollar limit, missing that ALL qualifying purchases this year count toward the phase-out threshold.Takes your other qualifying purchases as a separate input and applies the dollar-for-dollar phase-out to the combined total.
Over-large deductionTreats a deduction that exceeds income the same way for both elections.Flags bonus/MACRS excess as a net operating loss (NOL, up to 80% future use) and Section 179 excess as a SECTION 179 CARRYFORWARD (still income-limited every future year) — two different mechanisms.
Business-use cutoffApplies bonus depreciation or Section 179 to an asset at or below 50% business use.Flags the 50%-or-less case explicitly — that property needs the straight-line Alternative Depreciation System instead, which is out of scope here.
"Bigger is always better"Assumes maxing out bonus depreciation is always right, even in an expected loss year.Shows the Section 179 and plain-MACRS alternatives side by side, so a smaller, income-capped election is visible as an option, not just the biggest number.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Forgetting that the Section 179 phase-out is based on ALL qualifying purchases for the year, not just the one asset being considered. A hand estimate often checks a single purchase against the $2,500,000 (2025) limit and stops there, missing that other equipment bought the same year counts toward the $4,000,000 phase-out threshold too.

What's the second most common mistake?

Treating an over-large deduction the same way under both elections. A bonus-depreciation deduction that exceeds taxable income creates or increases a net operating loss (NOL), which can offset up to 80% of a future year's income. A Section 179 election that exceeds income instead produces a SECTION 179 CARRYFORWARD -- a different mechanism, still capped by income every future year it's used, with no 80% ceiling but no better guarantee of use. Confusing the two overstates how much benefit either path locks in immediately.

What eligibility mistake gets made most often?

Applying bonus depreciation or Section 179 to an asset used 50% or less for business. Both elections require MORE than 50% business use; at or below that line, the property must use the slower, straight-line Alternative Depreciation System instead -- a rule easy to skip when the arithmetic focuses on the dollar amount rather than the use percentage.

What planning mistake gets made most often?

Assuming bonus depreciation is always the better choice because it is bigger. Section 179 is elected asset-by-asset up to the annual limit, while bonus depreciation is all-or-nothing for an entire property class. A business expecting a loss year sometimes prefers a smaller, income-capped Section 179 election -- or electing out of bonus depreciation entirely -- to avoid creating a large NOL and instead preserve depreciation for a future, higher-income year.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return -- other deductions, credits, AMT, self-employment tax, luxury-auto depreciation caps, or state conformity to bonus depreciation, which varies widely by state. Both apply the same published federal rules to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal bonus-depreciation, Section 179, and MACRS rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers and elections before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
